summary: The machine has everything needed to start building the Node.js + Mongoose audit-trail sample against the reachable Azure DocumentDB cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI). The DocumentDB MCP server and a full set of service skills are installed and available to verify collections, indexes and query plans. Several model 'cold answers' were incorrect or outdated (mostly because they described Cosmos DB's older databaseAccounts / RU model or Amazon DocumentDB), and the report lists precise corrections and sources. Missing developer accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and a local CLI (mongosh) would speed iteration but are not blockers; a few small information gaps remain (e.g., concrete Node.js Entra-auth code examples).
summary_points: Build can start: Node 24, npx, az (signed in), docker, and the documentdb MCP server are available and the run-environment points at a reachable DocumentDB cluster via DOCUMENTDB_URI.

Key cold answers were frequently conflating Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model) or MongoDB/Amazon DocumentDB details with the new Azure DocumentDB service; these are corrected with Microsoft docs and local skills.

The installed DocumentDB skills (deployment, connection, indexing, vector-search, full-text) plus the documentdb MCP server provide the verification and guidance needed to create collections, create indexes, run aggregation pipelines and explain plans.
Missing accelerators: DocumentDB Agent Kit (would speed code-generation and templates) and mongosh (handy for manual checks); both are recommended but not blocking.

Two small information gaps remain: a ready-to-copy Node.js example showing Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication with the Mongo driver, and a pinned Mongoose/mongodb driver matrix for Node 24 — these must be decided by the builder before publishing the sample.
Verdict: ready_with_gaps — proceed, apply the corrections listed under Guidance For Builder, and optionally add the accelerators/tools mentioned.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run the Node.js sample, npm install, npx for starting tools and generators
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run or build the Node.js + Mongoose sample locally.
tools.workaround: Use a machine with Node.js >= 20 (Node 24 recommended) or run in a container that has Node installed.

tools.name: npx
tools.needed_for: Install/run MCP servers and any npx-based installers or templates (DocumentDB MCP, agent-kit installer, etc.)
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to run MCP servers or one-shot installers from the repo; would need to install packages globally or run npm scripts.
tools.workaround: Use npm install + node to run local tools, or install npx (comes with npm >= 7).

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, confirm provider registration and regions, and optionally run the DocumentDB CLI commands for cluster management or portal verification
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot inspect subnet/role/portal state or enable any cluster-level features; blockers for provisioning flows.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal for the same operations or ask an operator with az to run commands.

references.title: Azure CLI cosmosdb mongocluster command group

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optionally run the local DocumentDB Gateway container for offline development and integration tests
tools.impact_if_missing: Developer cannot run the local Gateway image for high-fidelity offline tests; must test against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Run and verify against the live cluster (the run-environment already supplies one).

tools.name: azd
tools.needed_for: Optional high-level template/CI/CD flow (not required for the sample itself)
tools.impact_if_missing: No effect on building a local sample; would be useful only if the builder wanted to include azd-based deployment in the repo.
tools.workaround: Use Bicep or Azure CLI or scripts in README; or install azd if you plan to include azd-driven deployment.

tools.name: bicep
tools.needed_for: Optional IaC path (Bicep templates) to provision clusters — the repository's deployment skill and examples use Bicep for reproducible infra
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run the local Bicep-based deploy script to create a cluster from this machine. Not required for this sample because a cluster is pre-provisioned.
tools.workaround: Use `az deployment group create --template-file main.bicep` on a machine that has bicep installed, or run the example Bicep from the portal. The sample does not need to provision a cluster.

tools.name: terraform
tools.needed_for: Optional IaC path if the builder wants to include Terraform templates
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run local Terraform-based provisioning from this machine. Not required for building the sample against the existing cluster.
tools.workaround: Use Bicep or az CLI, or run Terraform on another machine with Terraform installed.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Hand-check connectivity, inspect collections/indexes and run quick find/aggregate commands interactively against the cluster
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to perform quick manual checks; the MCP 'documentdb' server can perform the same programmatic inspections, but an interactive shell is convenient.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_aggregate, documentdb_list_indexes) or install mongosh.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification (list/create collections, create/list indexes, run aggregation and explain plans, sample documents). Required by the sample build for verification steps.
tools.detail: Available; provides 18 tools (list_databases, insert_documents, aggregate, create_index, explain_operation, etc.) — every call must pass connection_profile 'default'.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder couldn't programmatically verify what collections/indexes were created or run explain() to validate index usage.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh or the Azure portal to inspect collections and indexes, but the MCP server centralizes these checks.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative Microsoft documentation search (used to check facts and current recommendations)
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to ground claims in Microsoft Learn content during the build and review.
tools.workaround: Use web browsing to learn.microsoft.com, or include key doc links in the agent kit; but the learn MCP server is preferable for verified docs in agent flows.

tools.name: Installed DocumentDB skills (documentdb-azure-deployment, documentdb-connection, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-full-text-search, documentdb-driver, documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-mcp-setup, documentdb-security, documentdb-natural-language-querying, documentdb-query-optimizer, documentdb-query-optimization, documentdb-storage, documentdb-sharding, documentdb-monitoring)
tools.needed_for: Guidance and authoritative examples for deployment, connection tuning, indexing, vector search and local dev; used to produce code snippets, index shapes and best-practice instructions.
tools.detail: All listed DocumentDB skills are installed (see inventory).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack curated best-practice guidance and short-cuts (index shapes, connection patterns, local dev tips).
tools.workaround: Fallback to general MongoDB docs and Azure CLI docs; but the skills provide service-specific, up-to-date patterns.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — would speed code generation and include vetted templates and an installer; not installed.
Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit (documentdb MCP) is installed, so no action required.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are deployed as resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API such as 2025-09-01).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared resource provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical use of databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB led the model to return the older Cosmos DB resource type instead of the newer mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in IaC or CLI commands will target Cosmos DB account semantics (RU model) and not create the DocumentDB mongoClusters that the sample must use; deployment and API mismatches would block verification.
improvements: On the quickstart/overview page (Learn) show 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' prominently as the resource type for Azure DocumentDB clusters, and add an explicit note distinguishing it from 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (legacy Cosmos DB).
Update any agent skill samples that previously used databaseAccounts to include mongoClusters examples and a one-line deprecation note.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI, not a separate extension). Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides a dedicated CLI command group for mongo clusters (az documentdb mongocluster or az cosmosdb mongocluster in preview) and examples in the deployment skill use az resource create against resource-type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' or the az documentdb/az cosmosdb 'mongocluster' subgroup. The correct command group for clusters is the documentdb/cosmosdb mongocluster commands (preview extension/command group).
confusions.grounding_source: learn (az documentdb mongocluster docs) and documentdb-azure-deployment
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB flow used az cosmosdb create and databaseAccounts; the new vCore DocumentDB uses a mongocluster subgroup or az resource create with 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters', so a memory of 'az cosmosdb create' is outdated.
confusions.build_risk: Running az cosmosdb create will create/modify a Cosmos DB account (databaseAccounts) — wrong resource type — and will not produce the mongoClusters cluster the sample expects.
improvements: Add an explicit snippet in the Azure CLI quickstart that shows az documentdb mongocluster create (or az resource create --resource-type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) and mark the older az cosmosdb create path as for Cosmos DB databaseAccounts only.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep / ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account with kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities/settings for Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct resource type for Azure DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM templates), and Terraform uses the azurerm_mongo_cluster (or azapi targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) / AzAPI equivalents; older databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account refer to Cosmos DB databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-azure-deployment and Learn mongoClusters ARM/TF docs
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical overlap: Cosmos DB used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos accounts; the new vCore offering uses mongoClusters. The names are similar and the provider namespace is the same, causing confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in IaC would create a different service (Cosmos DB account); the sample must use mongoClusters to match the DocumentDB cluster described in the run environment.
improvements: Update the Bicep quickstarts to include a 'DocumentDB (mongoClusters)' example near the top and a clear disambiguation paragraph explaining which template to use for vCore DocumentDB vs the legacy databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB).

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-style URI for Cosmos Mongo API: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<authDB>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false. Username often includes the account (e.g. user@<account>) and SSL=true (TLS) is required. Port commonly 10255 for TLS endpoints.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB connection strings are Mongo-style SRV or standard URIs but use the DocumentDB cluster suffix and recommended parameters. Example form (from deployment/connection guidance): mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false (tls=true required; retryWrites should be false). The host suffix and SRV pattern differ from older Cosmos databaseAccounts hosts and port numbers.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recalled Cosmos DB's legacy Mongo endpoints and port (10255) instead of the newer DocumentDB SRV host suffix and documented tls/authMechanism guidance.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo connection string examples (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or wrong URI parameters (e.g., leaving retryWrites default) can cause authentication failures or connection errors at runtime.
improvements: Update the quickstart connection-string page to show the exact SRV and non-SRV examples used by Azure DocumentDB and call out retryWrites=false and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 explicitly.
In the documentdb-mcp-setup skill and docs, show the literal recommended placeholder pattern the sample should expect in DOCUMENTDB_URI.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput: Request Units per second (RU/s). You choose provisioned RU/s (manual or autoscale) or serverless where available. (No vCore-based tiers in the classic Cosmos DB model.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore offering) is billed and provisioned by compute tiers (vCores / named tiers like M10, M20, M30, ...). The RU model describes the Cosmos DB/RU sibling (Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)); DocumentDB uses a vCore/compute+storage pricing model instead.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing and compute model)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services are Mongo-compatible and historically Cosmos DB used RU billing; the model answered for Cosmos DB rather than the vCore DocumentDB service.
confusions.build_risk: Picking RU-based assumptions would lead to wrong recommendations for index/write-costs and capacity sizing; the sample must assume the run-environment's compute-tier model (M30 etc.).
improvements: Add a short comparison table on the DocumentDB overview page clarifying 'vCore compute tiers (M10..M200)' vs 'Cosmos RU model' to prevent confusion in quickstarts.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API you normally authenticate with account keys (primary/secondary keys) or Mongo-style database users (SCRAM credentials). Historically Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is not supported for the MongoDB API; drivers connect using the Mongo URI with username/password and TLS.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) credentials and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication and RBAC; the service exposes 'authMode' options (including 'MicrosoftEntraID') and the az/documentdb CLI and security guidance reference Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC as a supported authentication method. Drivers can obtain tokens and use Entra-auth modes per the service docs (the sample builder should follow documentdb-security guidance when Entra auth is required).
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-security and az documentdb CLI docs (auth-allowed-modes)

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (auth-allowed-modes includes MicrosoftEntraID)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos's Mongo API lacked Entra-based RBAC; the model recalled that older limitation rather than the newer DocumentDB capability which explicitly supports Entra in its auth modes.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming Entra auth is unavailable would make the sample avoid recommended enterprise authentication paths or force use of long-lived credentials; conversely assuming Entra when the cluster isn't configured for it will cause auth failures.
improvements: Add a short 'How to use Microsoft Entra ID with Node.js driver' example to documentdb-security or documentdb-connection documentation (a copy-paste code snippet would prevent confusion).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (for Node.js use the mongodb driver or Mongoose). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB SDK — you use Mongo-compatible drivers against the DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo endpoint.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use standard MongoDB drivers (Node.js: mongodb or Mongoose). There is no special proprietary SDK for the Mongo protocol; follow driver best practices (singleton MongoClient) per documentdb-driver/documentdb-connection guidance.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: I believe the service exposes vector index types such as HNSW and IVF via provider-specific index options on createIndex, but exact syntax varies. Example (my best guess): db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { name: "embedding_idx", vectorType: "hnsw", metric: "cosine", dims: 1536 }). NOTE: this syntax is vendor-specific and not standard MongoDB; treat as low-confidence.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index sub-types (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf) via its native cosmosSearch/vector index system and provides guidance and commands via createSearchIndexes / index-creation APIs; index creation and query syntax use the service's `createSearchIndexes` and `$search` pipeline (or documented admin commands), not standard createIndex with a 'vector' type.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed up community createIndex vector proposals and Atlas/other vendor syntaxes; DocumentDB uses its own cosmosSearch/vector index API and tooling.
confusions.build_risk: Using a createIndex-style command will fail; the builder must use the DocumentDB search/index command and the sample should follow the documentdb-vector-search guidance when vector features are needed.
improvements: Document a copy-paste vector-index snippet under the 'vector-search' quickstart that shows the exact createSearchIndexes JSON and a minimal query example using $search + cosmosSearch.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: For full-text you can use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })) for basic text search. For richer/hybrid (semantic + vector) search, Azure's recommended approach is to index Cosmos DB data into Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) and perform hybrid queries there; Mongo API doesn't provide Atlas Search-style built-in hybrid search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in full-text and hybrid capabilities via its search system: createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25), and hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector) is supported via the service's search index and $search semantics (no external search service required). The community $text index is NOT the DocumentDB search path.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older patterns used Azure Cognitive Search as an external index for Cosmos DB; the new DocumentDB includes first-class $search and vector capabilities, so the model's recollection of external Cognitive Search is outdated here.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos DB integration guides (historical pattern)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder designers the sample expecting to use external Azure Search, they'd add extra complexity; instead, use the integrated createSearchIndexes + $search per documentdb-full-text-search.
improvements: Add a 'hybrid search' short example page that shows a minimal end-to-end example of creating a search index (BM25 + vector), indexing sample docs and querying via $search with combined BM25+vector logic.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported protocol versions vary by account configuration; historically Cosmos DB's Mongo API provided compatibility with multiple Mongo versions (3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4, 5.0 in various SKUs). Some Mongo features are missing or emulated: server-side JS execution, certain storage-engine-specific features, and historically limited or no multi-document ACID transactions and limited aggregation stages/behaviour differences. Exact supported wire version must be checked against the account's configured Mongo version.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions (5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 per docs) and exposes a high degree of operator/feature coverage (compatibility docs show operator-level support); specific features vary by serverVersion setting and account tier — always check the cluster's serverVersion property. The service documents per-version operator compatibility and the serverVersion is configurable on cluster creation.
confusions.grounding_source: learn (MQL compatibility pages) and documentdb-azure-deployment (serverVersion property)

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model remembered an older Cosmos-era compatibility statement and mixed it with older MongoDB versions; the current DocumentDB docs explicitly enumerate supported wire/server versions and operator coverage.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API compatibility notes

confusions.build_risk: Assuming an unsupported operator or wrong server version could produce runtime errors; the builder must check the target cluster's serverVersion and consult the compatibility matrix.
improvements: Add a short 'compatibility at a glance' table to quickstarts for each supported serverVersion with common pitfalls (e.g., unsupported aggregation stages) and driver behavior guidance.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for local development (Windows; Docker support limited). Historically the emulator primarily targets the SQL API; MongoDB API support was limited. Best practical approach for Mongo-driver development is to run a local MongoDB server (official mongo Docker image) listening on 27017 for driver-level testing. The Cosmos emulator endpoint and ports differ (SQL endpoints use 8081); Mongo-compatible live testing generally requires a real Cosmos account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a local Gateway Docker image for development: ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local (Gateway) exposing the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256; use the Gateway image or docker-compose recommended in documentdb-local-deployment for high-fidelity local tests rather than a plain Mongo image if you need DocumentDB feature parity.

grounding_links.title: Local Gateway image and ports (DocumentDB local)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model recollected the Cosmos DB emulator limitations and generic Mongo local testing advice; DocumentDB ships a local Gateway image that is the recommended developer local runtime.
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain MongoDB server for local tests misses DocumentDB-specific features (cosmosSearch, vector indexes, serverVersion differences). Use the local Gateway when parity is needed.
improvements: On the DocumentDB quickstart, include a 'Local Gateway' quickstart snippet that shows the docker run/docker-compose minimal example with port 10260 and TLS flags.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams support on the MongoDB API has been limited historically. Many Cosmos Mongo API versions did not support change streams; if supported it depends on the account's MongoDB wire-version compatibility and may need an account-level feature flag. Assume not available unless the account explicitly advertises change stream support.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB; multi-shard change streams currently require a feature enablement (preview setting) for multishard clusters and you may need to enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature in the portal (Settings → Features) for cross-shard streams. The docs include examples and the resume semantics.
confusions.grounding_source: learn (change streams docs) and Mongoose+DocumentDB tutorial notes

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (how-to / enable multi-shard)
Mongoose tutorial notes referencing change streams

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically many Cosmos Mongo endpoints lacked full change-stream support; the new DocumentDB service provides change streams with clear enablement steps, but older knowledge (no change streams) persists in the model.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB docs with limited change stream support

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable, they'll miss opportunities for online migrations or real-time features; if the builder assumes multi-shard streams are enabled they may get a false-positive until the feature is turned on.
improvements: Make the portal feature flag location and CLI equivalent more prominent in the change streams doc (a single 'Enable multi-shard change streams' short paragraph with a portal screenshot and az CLI command).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection tools for Cosmos/Mongo-compatible accounts. The general azure MCP server provides broad Azure tooling but the documentdb MCP server contains service-specific inspectors and index/plan viewers for DocumentDB/Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the documentdb MCP server provides the data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, aggregate, explain_operation, create_index, list_indexes, etc.). The general azure MCP server complements it for control-plane operations and best-practice lookup but is not a substitute for the service-specific data-plane tooling.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-mcp-setup and the inventory's documentdb MCP server entry

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally named its original NoSQL offering Azure DocumentDB; that service evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure DocumentDB name historically referred to the SQL/Core API of Cosmos. This is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB; Cosmos DB is a Microsoft proprietary, multi-model database with API compatibility layers (SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but ambiguous: the name 'Azure DocumentDB' historically referred to the pre-Cosmos engine (which evolved into Cosmos DB). More recently, 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' was renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB' (vCore offering) and is a distinct, vCore-based service powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine. The new Azure DocumentDB is separate from Amazon DocumentDB and from the legacy DocumentDB->Cosmos renaming history; documentation explicitly calls out these distinctions.
confusions.grounding_source: Learn (DocumentDB naming & FAQ) and documentdb-azure-deployment release notes

grounding_links.title: documentdb release notes (rename from vCore Cosmos to Azure DocumentDB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' has been used at different times for different services (the original DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB, and the vCore rebranding of Cosmos DB for MongoDB). The model conflated these historical usages.
confusions.build_risk: Misstating the lineage could mislead builders about compatibility, pricing and migration expectations; use the run-environment guidance to pick the right API and pricing model.
improvements: Add an explicit 'naming timeline' box to the product overview that states '2014–2017: DocumentDB → renamed to Cosmos DB; 2025: Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) renamed to Azure DocumentDB (vCore) — these are distinct concepts)'.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API Cosmos DB uses Microsoft's Cosmos storage/engine and translates Mongo wire protocol calls to its internal engine. In most cases application code can use Mongo drivers unchanged, but some server-side behaviours, performance characteristics, and unsupported Mongo features (certain aggregation stages, server-side JS, cross-shard transactions, change streams) may require code changes or limitations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore offering) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (MIT-licensed) and in many cases application code can reuse MongoDB drivers unchanged. However there are operator-level/compatibility differences documented in the MQL compatibility matrix; check feature-level compatibility for the cluster's configured serverVersion. The implementation is not the original Cosmos engine; it’s the open-source DocumentDB engine and this can matter for features and portability.
confusions.grounding_source: learn (DocumentDB open-source engine docs) and documentdb-azure-deployment

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB open-source engine and implementation notes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model assumed the older Cosmos engine; the current service runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine and that changes some operational characteristics (compatibility matrix, vector and text search integration).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming Cosmos engine semantics could cause subtle runtime differences; the builder must validate operator compatibility for the target serverVersion.
improvements: Add a short 'compatibility checklist' on the quickstart that tells sample authors to run a one-line compatibility check against the target cluster before assuming a given operator or stage is supported.

confusions.question: Which client library and connection options will this sample use to connect to the DocumentDB cluster from Node.js?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Mongoose (npm package 'mongoose') and connect with mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, ssl: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', authSource: 'admin', retryWrites: false }). Read the full Mongo URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI; do not hard-code credentials. (If the cluster needs extra TLS CA configuration, pass tlsCAFile option.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Mongoose (mongoose) or the mongodb driver and pass the DOCUMENTDB_URI as provided; recommended options include tls/tls=true (or tls: true in driver options), authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256, and retryWrites=false. The exact SRV/non-SRV URI form and some option names differ from older Cosmos examples — follow documentdb-connection and documentdb-mcp-setup examples (they recommend mongodb+srv with tls=true and authMechanism SCRAM-SHA-256).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used legacy Cosmos connection-option names (ssl, replicaSet globaldb, port 10255) instead of the documented DocumentDB SRV recommendations and the service's authMechanism defaults. Option names in drivers have also evolved (tls vs ssl).
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong options (e.g., unsupported replicaSet name) can lead to connection failures; the sample should consume DOCUMENTDB_URI unchanged and pass driver options per documentdb-connection guidance.
improvements: Add an exact 'Node.js + Mongoose connection snippet' to the documentdb-connection skill with a SRV and non-SRV example and explicit recommended options for Node 24 + mongoose 7.x.

confusions.question: What index definition does the sample need to efficiently reconstruct a payment timeline?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a compound index on paymentReference and timestamp: db.collection.createIndex({ paymentReference: 1, stageTimestamp: 1 }). This supports the aggregation that matches by paymentReference and sorts by stageTimestamp.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — a compound index on { paymentReference: 1, stageTimestamp: 1 } is the recommended index shape to support the match+sort timeline aggregation and avoid collection scans.

confusions.question: How will the sample enforce immutability (prevent updates) at the application layer?
confusions.cold_answer: Implement Mongoose schema-level guards: set schema pre-hooks for updateOne, updateMany, findOneAndUpdate, replaceOne to throw an error; in pre('save') allow only docs where doc.isNew === true and throw on attempted resave. Optionally expose only an insert API and never call update operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and recommended: implement application-layer guards (Mongoose pre hooks for update operations and pre-save checks) and expose an insert-only API. This aligns with documentdb-data-modeling and driver best practices. The sample should use both schema immutability where available and pre-hooks for the update operation names Mongoose invokes.

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will the sample expose to reconstruct the full timeline for a payment reference?
confusions.cold_answer: Pipeline: [ { $match: { paymentReference: '<ref>' } }, { $sort: { stageTimestamp: 1 } }, { $group: { _id: '$paymentReference', timeline: { $push: { stage: '$stage', metadata: '$metadata', timestamp: '$stageTimestamp', docId: '$_id' } } } } ]. The API will accept a paymentReference, substitute it into $match, run the pipeline and return the timeline array.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — match by paymentReference, sort by recorded timestamp, then $group with $push is a straightforward pipeline to reconstruct the ordered timeline. The sample can return the $push array or just a $sort + $project to return documents in order; ensure the compound index (paymentReference + stageTimestamp) exists for efficiency.

confusions.question: What exact DOCUMENTDB_URI format will the sample expect in the environment so it can connect without hard-coded values?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect a Mongo-style URI template in DOCUMENTDB_URI, for example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/admin?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false. The sample will pass this URI straight to mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, {...}).
confusions.grounded_answer: The sample should expect a Mongo-style connection string but use the DocumentDB cluster form. Recommended patterns in skills and MCP setup are SRV or non-SRV URIs like: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false or the non-SRV equivalent with tls=true. The sample must read DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it through unchanged to mongoose.connect and apply DocumentDB-specific driver options (tls, authMechanism, retryWrites=false) if necessary.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used legacy Cosmos DB host suffix and ports instead of the DocumentDB SRV host suffix and recommended tls/authMechanism parameters.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample's .env.example recommends the old Cosmos URI form, users will fail to connect; the sample must show the SRV pattern and note the tls/authMechanism/retryWrites settings.
